speechtext:
I would hope it is, because that is the work that is being done by the board, and I think the press is 'becoming increasingly conscious of the value of some parts of the board's work.
I should like to refer to the report of his visit to the board made by Mr. Norman Smith of the Ottawa Journal and appearing in the Ottawa Journal of April 20, 1943. He said:
The weakest thing about our whole publicity scheme in the United States is that there are not offices in Chicago and San Francisco as well.

War Appropriation-External Affairs
The men in New York and Washington are certainly working hard and most people down here believe they are working effectively.
Their salaries, some of them, look big from Ottawa, but with the cost of living as it is here and considering the nature of their work it is probable that most of them should be getting more rather than less.
There is no lack of documentary proof that they are getting good publicity in the papers, the movies, over the radio and the public platform. Nor is there lack of indication where and when they have prevented bad publicity, arrested harmful thought trends or planted helpful ones. The set-up could be improved- what set-up couldn't be improved?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I hope they inform the people of the United States that all the snow has gone from here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
A similar article by Mr. Arthur R. Ford, editor in chief of the Free Press, of London, appeared in that paper on May 7, 1943. Mr. Ford is president of the Canadian Press, and in a lengthy article he refers to the work of the board. He says:
Now we come to Canada which was the last country to set up a department of information in Washington. I have been rather doubtful of the value of such a bureau. However, after seeing the Washington bureau in operation I am inclined to change my mind.
So I submit to the committee that the work of the board in the United States has been useful beyond words in giving facts about Canada. There has been no element of propaganda about it from beginning to end. We have nothing to tell the United States except the facts and to see that they are attractively presented. That is the whole purpose of this agency, and it has no other purpose. It has never been under any suspicion of having any other purpose. It could not have any other purpose.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that there is no element of propaganda in it. Is not the whole thing propoganda, to make the people of the United States understand what Canada is doing?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If my hon. friend uses the word "propaganda" in that sense, which is its true literal sense, I agree with him. But propaganda has in addition certain unfavourable connotations, and I do not use the word for that reason.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: When it is tinged politically it becomes objectionable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If my hon. friend means propaganda in its true literal sense, meaning to propagate information, I am completely in agreement with him.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am glad we agree on something.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In addition, the board has established an office in the United Kingdom-with a staff of four-and one in Canberra. The office in the United Kingdom has cooperated very fully with the public relations officers of the armed services-under the direction of Mr. J. W. G. Clark-who have done such an exceedingly good job in making available to the Canadian public information about the work of our boys overseas and at sea. The hon. member for Peterborough West asked what we were doing in South America.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is the wartime information board doing toward acquainting the members of our armed forces overseas with general developments so far as our nation here is concerned? I think my hon. friend-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I shall come to that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am sorry; I did not know that was on the agenda.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, it is, but I thought I should deal with the other first.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am sorry I interrupted.	.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think I should deal with the question asked by the member for Peterborough West, because it brings up an extraordinarily interesting matter which the board has very much in mind. The organization to deal with South America is headed by Mr. Allan Anderson, who for fourteen years was correspondent of the Southam newspapers in South America.
Mr. FPiASER (Peterborough West): He speaks Spanish?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Oh, yes. I am sorry; he was not for fourteen years in South America, but he had just returned from South America where he was correspondent for the Southam press when he assumed responsibility for the board's work there. He speaks Spanish fluently and has a working knowledge of Portuguese. His secretary also speaks Spanish and has a working knowledge of Portuguese.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What is a working
knowledge?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It means that he can read it and make himself understood on social occasions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not very fluent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Not very fluent, but able to get by with it, as a good many hon. members do with the other language in Canada. He has another assistant, born in

War Appropriation-External Affairs
the Argentine, who speaks Spanish and French fluently and has some Italian and Portuguese. Their job is to send out articles and press releases, and they send them in Spanish. They do not send them broadcast. They send them only to newspaper editors with whom they have already established personal contacts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Where is he located?
Mr. CLAXTO'N: In Ottawa. In parenthesis, I should say that the emphasis of the board has varied since being an agency which at the beginning, and quite rightly, distributed large quantities of material to the public. The present emphasis in the work of the board is to give material to meet a demand that exists and a need that has been expressed, and that policy is followed in connection with the distribution of news material and articles to the South American press.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Are these articles to which the hon. gentleman refers as being sent out in Spanish by Mr. Anderson and his staff prepared by the board, or are they the articles that come through from the press men attached to the different departments?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
These articles are
specially prepared by the board, but frequently the work is that of editing other articles from government departments or from other agencies in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That does not quite coincide with what the hon. gentleman said a little while ago, that these articles were not prepared by the board but that a personal service was performed in New York. I understood that these articles were all canned stuff prepared by the fifty-seven varieties of press agents attached to the different departments. That is what the public thinks anyway.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend will forgive me if I say that there is a difference between the material sent out from Canada to South America and the material that is sent from Canada to the United States. Material from Canada to the United States naturally is news which goes out through the ordinary agencies, and the work of the board is to assist the flow of that news; whereas, so far as material going to South America is concerned, it must be remembered it is already serviced by news agencies from the United States and other countries, and anything that we could send would not be news in that sense. So that the articles are more background material giving long-term information.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They are special articles, then?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Specially prepared by the board?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, or possibly by somebody else for the board, or else material is used obtained from other government departments and services or from other newspapers in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What control does the board exercise over writers or authors whose services. it secures for the writing of articles? During the past few months some fourteen authors or writers in this country have written articles for the board. What control does the board exercise over the information contained in those articles?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It would be more convenient if I were allowed to finish one subject at a time. At present I am dealing with South America, and if my hon. friend would forgive me and remind me of that later, in case I forget, I should be glad.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It fits into the discussion on South America just the same.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
He was speaking of
special articles, and so are you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I was speaking about
Latin America in reply to a question. All articles sent to South America are prepared by the board, as far as I know. They are prepared or edited and the board takes full responsibility for them. They are not broadcast but sent to newspaper editors and publishers with whom Mr. Anderson himself has already established contacts, or to one of the south American editors who visited Canada, or to a Canadian legation for use through the legation, or to a branch of a Canadian bank for use in such ways as they may see fit. But they are not sent to any others.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is any information sent to South America by means of any shortwave American station?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I understand it has been, but there is not a regular service.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We have no facilities
here, but I thought it might have been done through an American short-wave station.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
As part of this work, and in order to establish better associations and more friendly relations with South America, a number of south American editors have visited Canada. The total is fifty-nine, representing ten countries, and I suppose that all

War Appropriation-External Affairs
of them have written, for their own publications as well as others, stories about Canada on their return to their own countries. In addition, several of them broadcast from Canada. I assume that these broadcasts must have been sent at some stage by short wave, but the exact technical operation I cannot describe. I believe that one writer has indicated his intention to write a book about Canada. There will be a special Canadian number of a publication having distribution all over South America. I refer to Norte.
There is another branch of work in South America and that is what may be called background information. This is under the direction of Mr. Malcolm Ross, who has a working knowledge of French, German and Spanish. He has had to do with arranging for broadcasts, and already one thirty-minute programme has been sent to the Argentine, Colombia, Cuba, Mexico and Peru. Some programmes have been prepared and are broadcast from south American countries. Arrangements are being made for programmes of music and talks to be given in each of the Latin American countries on their day of independence.
Then in the way of films, paid for by the wartime information board and made by the national film board, fourteen commercial films have been exhibited in South America, of which eleven. I think, were of the "World in Action" series. There are eight more in preparation. These are distributed through an agency, United Artists World corporation, and they are available to 4,000 theatres in Latin America. They have Spanish and Portuguese sound tracks. We know that 400 theatres in Mexico have taken those films. The leader of the opposition will appreciate that we are doing a good deal to prepare for the day when the short-wave station which he has had at heart will be in operation; there will be friendly contacts established with numerous South Americans, and there will be in Canada the small nucleus of a staff who can help to prepare the programmes for such a station. The work is well in hand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I apologize for interrupting my hon. friend so often, but I think it advisable to ask questions when his points arise, one by one. Do I take it that we have no representatives of the wartime information board on the ground in South America? If this is so, apparently the distribution of films for propaganda purposes and the dissemination of information, such as the hon. member has described, must all be done from here. If so, what is the normal channel through which this information goes? Does it go through the trade commissioners in the various
centres in South America, or through the legations which have been set up in various South American republics?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: With regard to the films-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt, but the hon. member has spoken for forty minutes. However I take it that the committee will allow him to go on for another forty minutes if necessary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We are in
committee. As long as anyone intervenes, he may resume.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I believe I have eased
that situation now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The films for South America, fourteen so far and eight under preparation, are distributed there, as I have just said, by United Artists World Corporation, which is a commercial agency. These films are commercial films; they are shown in the commercial picture theatres, and it is in the interests of the agency distributing them to see that they get the widest possible distribution. In addition, however, the visits to which I have referred result in contacts being made which are used so that the representatives of the two countries cooperate in pushing their wares in each of their countries; that is the advantage of personal association. Also we 'now have three legations in South America, and each of these is helping very materially in these respects.
I have only one further word to say about the South American scene. A trial set of books about Canada has been put together through the cooperation of the publishers to whom we are grateful for contributing the books free, the National Gallery, who contributed reproductions of pictures free, and the film board, who contributed "stills" about Canada. These have been put together, with a great deal of other material, including posters. One set, I believe, has been sent to Chile. Two other sets are in course of preparation to be sent to the Argentine and Brazil. If the war information board had to pay for all that material the cost would aggregate, I believe, more than a thousand dollars a set. I understand that a good deal of this is contributed, so that expense is not borne by us. It is of the nature of an experiment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Where will they be placed in Chile?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In the principal libraries, museums and other public centres. They will be exhibited in one place and then move into another, just as exhibitions of pictures



War Appropriation-External Affairs
rotate from place to place. They were asked for by our minister to Chile to meet demands which he had for further information about Canada, and arrangements for their distribution and display will be made through him.
That concludes what I was to say about the work of the wartime information board abroad. Now just a word about its work at home.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said that all the news sent to South America is in Spanish; therefore Brazil would not get any of it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If I said Spanish, I was right, but it is put into Portuguese for distribution in Brazil. It is sent in Spanish to Brazil, and arrangements are made locally for its translation into Portuguese before it is distributed to the Brazilian newspapers and other recipients.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Has the board made use of the news item feature in the picture houses, both in the United States and in South America, to introduce Canadian news?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is done by the
national film board, and my information is that it is made use of extensively, and, as my hon. friend's question suggests, it is an extraordinarily useful means of publicity.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Before the hon. member leaves the work of the board in other parts, may I remind him that, so far as I know, ae has not said anything about how far the board has gone with respect to introducing news features and propaganda generally in Mexico. That country has been before the house more emphatically perhaps during the last few days than hitherto, because of the Prime Minister's statement in regard to exchange of diplomatic representation. Nor has the hon. member mentioned any part of the empire other than the United Kingdom with respect to the work of the wartime information board. Has anything been done with respect to South Africa or Australia or New Zealand?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: To answer the third question first, we have, as I think I have mentioned, a representative of the board at Canberra, Australia, and I have seen reports from the Canadian high commissioner there that he is doing extraordinarily useful work.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The Canadian high commissioner does a little work on his own, too.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He certainly does.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Does the wartime information board take full responsibility for his statements?
fMr. C'.axton.]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not entirely, just credit. With regard to the suggestion that this work may extend to other parts of the world, a good deal of material is sent out either through the office of war information broadcasts or through British ministry of information broadcasts, by cooperation, but it is impossible for the board to have representatives in any other countries without the house granting the board some more money. This costs money.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
You might cut down on
some items and extend others.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend would find it difficult to cut down on any
of the items.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The main thing after all is to develop proper information in the United States; is not that the real purpose of this board?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is a principal
purpose.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If it were not for that you would not have it at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would not go so far as to say that, but I would say that it is a very large part of the purpose.
With regard to Mexico I did mention that we have shown these films of the national film board, paid for by the wartime information board, to four hundred theatres in Mexico, and the same close relationships of our representatives with newspaper men and publishers exist in Mexico as in other countries. A considerable number of Mexican newspaper men are included in the list that was given to me. Between December 4 and 8 there was a visit to Canada by eight Mexican newspaper men, who travelled extensively throughout the country'.
Now with regard to the home front-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman leaves that point, do you also send literature to Central America, to San Salvador, Costa Rica, and so on?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes; I should have said this included1 Latin America, and I intended to cover that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You mentioned South America but did not include Central America.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should have included it, because the work has been carried on equally there.
With regard to the home front, I have already indicated the change in emphasis from the distribution of material to a concentration on facilitating the flow of news, particularly with relation to the work abroad; but in

War Appropriation-External Affairs
addition a great deal more has been done in Canada. There has been'instituted a reports branch of the wartime information board, the main purpose of which is to find out what the information is, what to say and how it should be said, and to advise other government departments. That work has been extensively carried on in that indirect way. This reports branch also cooperates with the censorship authorities in the reading of publications issued in Canada, including all the foreign language press, for censorship and wartime information purposes, some eight employees being engaged in that work.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What about the activities of the board within Canada in disseminating information, we will say with respect to the buying of victory bonds and that sort of thing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
As I think my hon. friend knows, the national war finance committee handles its own publicity. However, there are coordinating committees, on which the wartime information board is represented, which endeavour to coordinate the activities of all the various publicity agencies working in connection with the war.
My hon. friend asked what was being done to keep the troops informed about news of Canada. Recently there has been issued a publication called "Canadian Affairs," the first number of which was published on May 1 of this year by the wartime information board for the Department of National Defence. The first issue ran to some twenty-five thousand copies; it was printed in England and distributed to the armed forces of Canada overseas. I have a copy of that publication here which hon. members may see if they wish. Following the publication of this first issue General McNaughton sent the board a telegram of congratulation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: How often is it issued?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is issued fortnightly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Did my hon. friend say how that pamphlet was distributed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is distributed to the armed forces in England and overseas.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Entirely?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is not a news distribution; it is instructional, for the Canadian armed forces overseas?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not instructional, informative.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That was the information I got, that it was instructional for the Canadian armed forces overseas.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am sorry; that is right, instructional in the informative sense. For example, the first number contained an article headed " Canada in the Fourth Year of War." That and other articles may be used by officers for the purpose of talks to their own men, and in that sense it is instructional.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Something like "Canada at War," only for use over there?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Except that the matter in the numbers I have seen is much less limited to information and is devoted more to matters of opinion and to reporting on trends in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does it give any information as to the numbers and the activities of the home army?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have not seen any. Then in addition the board still publishes "Canada at War." This is a work that has been carried on from the previous agencies. Of this publication 93.000 copies are printed in English and 27,000 in French, which are sent out only in answer to requests. The mailing list is cleaned out every five or six months, by sending circulars asking if people want to receive the publication. If they do not, it is not sent to them any longer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is a question I have asked before in regard to "Canada at War" to which I have not yet received an answer. In January and February of this year this publication contained full information in regard to the intake into the armed forces, the operation of the call-up, the number of medical examination notices sent out, the number who answered the call, and general information with regard to the requisition, by military districts, of man-power; the numbers who reported for training and the percentage accepted as per requisition. That was very useful information; it gave a picture of the military situation in Canada; province by province, military district by military district, it gave a picture of the operation of the National Resources Mobilization Act. That has been deleted from the issues of March, April, May and June. I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary why it was deleted, and whether it is intended that this information is to be discontinued. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this is the only way the people of Canada may know just how well the armed forces are being kept up to strength and how the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act are being applied.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
With regard to films: during this period the wartime information board has paid for a number of films which have been produced by the national film board. Altogether there have been some 74 films, representing a total cost over the period of 8675,348.10. Those films have had an extensive distribution in the United States, Canada and other countries. For example the "Canada Carries On" series has had a nominal distribution in Canada of 2,250.000. It also was distributed to 96 different territories, including South Africa and other countries, and in twelve different languages. Those films had a non-theatrical distribution of over a million. The series "The World in Action" had a distribution of 2,250,000 in Canada. Eight of those films were distributed to 6,000 United States theatres, and three of them went to 500 United Kingdom theatres. In addition the wartime information board facilitated the production of a picture used in the victory loan campaign, of which 274 prints were made. It has produced posters and pamphlets. It has handled the visits of distinguished persons and visiting journalists such as I have indicated. It has cooperated with other government departments, notably with the public relations officers of the armed services, and

War Appropriation-External Affairs
in other ways it has carried on much the same work that had been done by the division of public information in Canada, its predecessor.
A word with regard to staff. The staff today numbers 132. At the end of August, 1942, when the division of public information operated, there was a total staff of 158, including casual workers. So that the staff during this period has decreased by no less than 26. These 132 members of the staff are divided between nineteen abroad, and the remainder at home.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Most of those abroad are in the United States.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Eleven are in New York and three at Washington. The board is continually asked to take on extra work of a direct publicity character. It can do so only with additions to staff and additional money.
I ask hon. members to consider the size of the staff, and for a minute to compare it with the staff of the ministry of information in Great Britain which, as of February 1, 1943, numbered 2.824. At that time there were in other British government departments, staffs totalling 1,038; but to these figures should be added the staff of the ministry of information in the United States, totalling on April 21, 1943, a personnel of 537.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Was that staff sent from Canada, or were they engaged in the United States?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am referring to the British Ministry of Information. So that if the British staff of 537 in the United States is compared with the Canadian staff of 14, the difference is at once apparent. The British staff in the United States is four times the total Canadian staff in all countries. The total British staffs engaged in this work stand at 3,361 or about 25 times the total staffs engaged in similar work in Canada.
Comparisons with the office of war information in the United States are difficult because of the recent reduction made in the office of war information. The last figures before the reduction showed a total staff of 4,800 of which 1,600 were engaged in domestic work. But to those should be added staffs of 153 government departments, totalling 2,895 full-time workers and 31,618 part-time workers.
The best information we have concerning Australia is that their information service carries a total personnel of 200. In South Africa it is 50. There are special reasons which will be appreciated by hon. members
why the Canadian staff should be larger, rather than smaller as it is, in proportion to other staffs. For one thing, our country is wide in extent. Then, we have two languages. Forty-one members of our staff are Frenchspeaking. In addition, we have to deal with our information needs in a nation of 130,000,000 people living next to us. So that it might have been understandable if the Canadian staff had been higher, in proportion, than the staffs of other countries. The fact is however that it is very much lower, in proportion, than the staff of any other country.
May I say a word with regard to salaries. At the time the wartime information board took over from the division of public information, salaries were approximately 820,000 a month. To-day, since adding the offices at Washington, New York, London and Canberra, with a staff of 19, and at a total cost per month of some $8,500 for overseas services alone, the total salaries roll per month is $22,000. So that despite these additions at New York, London, Canberra and Washington the payroll has increased by only $2,000 per month. In other words this additional service is being rendered at that small additional cost, while the actual cost of the additional officers in the four places I have mentioned is no less than $8,500 a month.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Perhaps we might clear up these points as we go along, if an interruption would not interfere with the hon. member's line of thought. Had the men who were connected with the wartime information board remained with the press, doing the ordinary work of the press, their salaries would have been very considerably lower than the salaries paid to men on the board carrying corresponding responsibility. Who fixed these salaries? In their fixation, why were they not frozen, as the salaries have been of men who have remained with the regular newspapers? We find however that salaries on the board are in many cases considerably higher. It would be interesting to know the basis upon which these salaries were determined.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am quite prepared to discuss each case at any length my hon. friend desires, but that is the situation. I would point out that in some cases these men were first employed by the division of public information which was taken over by the wartime information board, and others were in the government service at the outbreak of the war.

I have five in mind.
They are A. J. McKenna, Leonard Knott, Bruce West, E. G. Smith and N. Morant. There are two who are not officials of the wartime information board at all, Mr. J. W. G. Clark and Mr. Gerald Brown. These gentlemen are employees of the departments of national defence.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not refer to them as belonging to the wartime information board; I referred to them as belonging to other departments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not know how my hon. friend referred to them, but they would not be under the estimates we are considering at the moment. There were four who were appointed by the board to the staff at Ottawa and eight to the staff at Washington, so that there are twelve who were appointed by the wartime information board among those mentioned by the hon. member for Lake Centre. When Mr. Vining was appointed chairman of the wartime information board in September, 1942, he decided to get the best people he could for the job and he did succeed in getting a number of people to work for nothing or for expenses. He has told me, and I believe it to be true, that in every case he worked on the principle that a man should not receive more than he was receiving before. My information is that in every case that is what happened.
fMr. R. B. HaDSon.]

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does that apply to persons in the United States as well as those in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is the information which I have received from Mr. Vining. In his statements to the house on April 7 and May 19, my hon. friend gave the salaries of these various officials in Canadian dollars. Anyone reading those figures would think that the people were in receipt of sums of money which would enable them to buy that many dollars' worth of goods.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That was in the government return.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. The figures I gave were in accordance with the return brought down to the house, and I accepted the figures given by the department.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not suggest that the figures were wrong; I am explaining the figures given by my hon. friend and the form in which he gave them. Of course those were the figures which the public of Canada would be charged for these services, but in the case of the eight men working in the United States it must not be thought that they receive that amount of money. Actually they receive payment in United States dollars, and the purchasing power of that dollar is probably thirty per cent less to-day than it is in Canada for persons on an equivalent standard of living. I refer particularly to those in New York and Washington. They were not as well off as they would have been had they been working in Canada for the same salary.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would they have to pay as much income tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is a difficult point. I believe that all the temporary employees are subject to income tax in the United States, but not at the same rates as would apply in Canada. The permanent employees do not pay income tax in the United States, but there are only one or two in that class. That is taken into account in fixing the salaries. I will be glad to look into this.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is that not an answer to my hon. friend's argument when he tried to establish a point against the hon. member for Lake Centre? You must t-hke into consideration the cost of living when you are dealing with a matter of this kind. I think my hon. friend had better leave it as it was in the first instance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am willing to leave it
that way, provided you take into account the

War Appropriation-External Affairs
cost of living, the rates of pay and the income tax differential. If that is done I think without exception it will be found that these people working in the United States are worse off than if they were working in Canada and in receipt of the same salary.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is
a matter of calculation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is a matter of calculation, of estimation and of the difference in standards of living. But I believe it is true. As I have said, Mr. Vining endeavoured to apply, and I think succeeded in applying, the principle that no one should receive more than he got before. This is borne out by such investigations as I have been able to make.
Just a word in conclusion about the question of expenditures. On May 20, 1943, the hon. member was referring to the expenditures of the board, reported on page 2827 of Hansard as follows:
The situation is this, that in the first year of the war the former war information board, the bureau of public information, expended $202,672; whereas this new body has expended, during a period of a little over six and a half months, the sum of $579,000.
And a little later on he said that there had been a tremendous increase in the expenditures on publicity under this board. That left the impression that there had been a tremendous increase in the expenditures of the board during the time the board had been in existence. The hon. member took the figure $202,672, the expenditures for the first year of the bureau, and contrasted them with the last six months. He might just as well have taken the year before the war and compared it with 1942-43, because in the year before the war there were no expenditures whatever. The board and the war were getting going. It was like comparing the pre-war expenditure of Canada on the war or on munitions and supply or on anything else with the expenditure in the current year. But comparing what is comparable, namely, expenditures in the year preceding the board, my hon. friend will see that in the year 1942-43 the estimates brought down under the war appropriation bill amounted to $1,345,500. The figure my hon. friend got in a return for expenditures during six months, pretty nearly seven months, was $579,000. If he will compare the expenditures of $579,000 with an estimate of $1,345,500, he will see that in the last six months during which the board was operating it was spending at a lower rate than was provided for in the estimates, and at a lower rate than that
at which the division of public information
was spending, which the board succeeded on September 9, 1942.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That may only show that it was a reckless estimate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend has no justification for saying that. It is not borne out by the facts. The estimate was not so reckless, because, despite the increased expenditures on films, the total expenditure for the fiscal year 1942-43 will be in the neighbourhood of $1,400,000 to $1,500,000.
For this year we are setting down in the estimates the figure of $658,000, a substantial decrease from the figure for last year. That decrease is in part effected through the expenditure formerly provided for of $575,000 for films being taken into the estimates of the national film board. It was thought that that was the better way to do it. In addition there have been decreases right from the beginning of the wartime information board on September 9, 1942, and the proportionate part of the expenditure for the fiscal year 1942-43 expended since the institution of the board on September 9, 1942, is less than it should be, taken for the full year. So that my hon. friend's accusation of very high and rapidly increasing expenditures is not borne out, if it is related to the period immediately under review and the period preceding it, as it should be.

speechtext: I cannot follow my hon. friend's mathematics at the moment, but I should like information in connection with the expenditure. The total expenditure, as the hon. gentleman mentions, for the first six and a half months, was approximately $579,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: For the last six and a half months.

speechtext: The details are: salaries, $119,209.26; travelling expenses, $21,194.76; printing of pamphlets, $32,405.54; radio programmes, $11,765.28. That is the big item, and I think the committee should have a general analysis of that very large figure for miscellaneous expenditures. While I am on my feet theiti is something more.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
May I finish? I am nearly through. I shall be glad to put that break-down on Hansard, with the consent of the committee, if my hon. friend wants it.

The main reason for the difference, of course, is that the return did not ask for information that brought out specific expenditure on motion pictures. The expenditure on motion pictures during that period -was $261,073.03. That will give my hon. friend the information he vrants almost in a sentence, and clear up this very large item to which he refers, which undoubtedly puzzled him.
The budget that is being asked for is $658,000, and if increased demands are made on the board for additional work, I have no doubt" that sum of money will not be found to be sufficient. Additional staff will be required. But that is the figure that seems to be sufficient now. If we compare that figure with the expenditure on the previous year's operations of the combined division of public information and the wartime information board we will see that it represents a considerable decrease, a decrease of between $100,000 and $200,000, in addition to the decrease credited to films alone.
There is no better way of judging the usefulness of expenditures of this kind than by seeing that we get value for the money expended. I submit to this committee, and I think now I can submit to anyone else with confidence, that the value of the work being done by the board abroad and at home shows that this money is well spent. It was spent to meet a need that was felt before, and which would immediately exist again if it had not been met by the board. The events of the last few days indicate how useful has been the cooperation of the press relations officers, the press associations, the correspondents of newspapers overseas, with the wartime information board at various points in the background, in seeing that the people of this continent got early news of the landing in Sicily, and also that the statements which were made have afterwards received early and favourable notice in the United States both, in the press and over the radio.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is the wartime information board taking credit for all that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not suggest that. I said it had contributed to it by its work in the background, by making arrangements.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The newspapers would have got it if there had been no board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Honestly I cannot think that. Contrast the treatment that has been given in the United States, for example, to other stories that have broken, and you will see that something has happened.'

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If you get a good story the press will see that it is distributed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There have been good stories before which did not receive the attention they should have. I do not suggest that there is anything miraculous about this, but there has been hard work in the background.
Another method of appreciating the work of the board in addition to the value received, is to compare the work of the board and the expenditure of the board with the work done by other agencies. If my hon. friends would think of the proportionate figure of expenditure on the wartime information board in Canada and on corresponding agencies in Britain and the United States or Australia, and relate them in some way that is fair-I suggest to them the total expenditure on war-they will arrive at some astonishing figures.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In making that comparison you would have to take into consideration the officials connected wfith information branches in the Department of Finance, the Department of Labour, the Department of Munitions and Supply, the Department of National Defence, the Department of National Defence for Air, and the nineteen press agents connected with the wartime prices and trade board. Has the minister a record of the expenditure being made by press units in these various other departments? That is the only way to get a fair comparison.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have taken that into consideration very fully, and the hon. member will find that in Canada the number of such outside officers, outside the regular wartime information board, is very much smaller in proportion than the number of outside officers in every other country. The figures I will give exclude those outside officers in all countries. I think that was the right way to do it.
Mr. DIEFENBAIvER: Has the parliamentary assistant a statement with regard to expenditures for information in these other departments?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend suggested originally that the test was not the amount spent, or the comparable amount in relation to general war expenditures, but the value received. If he is to use one argument on one occasion, he should use it on the other.

We have done so because it was brought up in discussion before and there has been misinformation about the wartime information board. I hope that members of the house, the press and the public will not only appreciate that, but support it in every way they can, not merely by helpful and constructive work, but also by their criticisms.

speechtext:
I have been watching this particular department ever since this war started. It has been under several ministers, and I do not see how the parliamentary assistant can succeed with it at nearly the end of the fourth year of the war, after others have failed.
We do not need all this advertising in the United States. Britain tried it for a hundred and forty years, and did she educate them over there? No; they were isolationists for two years after the war began. This work was formerly in charge of the Minister of National War Services, now Mr. Justice J. T. Thorson. The similar organization in England is the most controversial government body in the old country to-day. It is linked up with the BBC, and both are con-tinously under fire in the British House of Commons on the ground that much of the information they disseminate is not information at all.
What have we in connection with this organization? Its spokesman here is the present 'parliamentary assistant, who made an address in the house, of which I have taken note, on May 29, 1942. I am not permitted to read from this address this session, but I can tell you that only last week or this

War Appropriation-External Affairs
present week one of the editors of the Montreal Standard was appointed by the parliamentary assistant to an important position in this branch.
Before this war started, I called the attention of the house, when I was sitting at this end of the chamber, to the need of educating first our own people in Canada and of giving them information before giving it to another country, even our great ally to the south.
The British office of information started in the early days of the war and was in charge of various ministers before being entrusted to Mr. Brendal Bracken by Mr. Churchill. They went to work and scattered over Germany millions of tracts and treatises as war information with the idea of trying to convert the German people. The campaign was so ridiculous that it failed. Then they worked the same thing with the BBC, one of whose heads, Mr. Peterson, had remarked a month or two before the war started that anyone preaching rearmament should be put in gaol and fed on bread and water. Would that Kipling were alive to-day 1 I believe he lived in the United States for over twenty years, and he could give more information about publicity in relation to our own nation and that of our great ally than anybody connected with the wartime information board.
The question is, what is information and what is not information? Who is to judge? Is it to be some member of the government or every member of the government? If its purposes are to dispense information, it should be non-political; it should be concerned wholly with the war. The complaint and the main attack made in the British House of Commons was that the propaganda to supply information and convert the people of the United States was political and was valueless. Money spent on this kind of propaganda is simply wasted.
As I said before the war started, when we were in the tide of the status campaign which began ten or fifteen years ago, Canada was a nation on the front pages of the United States magazines and at five o'clock teas and ten o'clock dinners in Washington, and by status we had got nowhere before the war.
If we want to distribute information, let us start with Canada and supply information to our own people. Ask any citizen of this country whether in the three years before the war and during the war we have not received less information than any other people. After all is said and done, it is the function of the press and not of the government of the day to give to the public this sort of information. The very fact of the establishment of this branch of government shows lack of understanding and appreciation and of confidence
in the function of the press. What do you do? You go to work and summon and appoint editors from all over the country. Some of them come in for a month or two and then resign. You bring them from the coast, the prairies, the east, and other places to gather information. Information as to what? As to the conduct of the war? Take as an illustration the Dieppe raid. Why should all these textbooks be written? Department stores are full of these productions, and parents of boys who fell at Dieppe tell me that they object to the class of information contained in books written by men some of whom were away out in the English channel and not on the shore at all during the engagement.
This kind of thing did not go on in the last war and it should not be encouraged now. When information should be given, the appropriate government officials representing the army, navy and the air force overseas should, under proper regulations, supply it to the proper authorities at the front and let it be sent across the ocean to Canada.
Before the war started we could get no information at all. As I said in this house on March 21, 1939, quoting the words of Prime Minister Chamberlain at that time, if the people are not allowed to know the facts; if they are given only so much as their rulers want them to know, then we are embarked on a course fraught with grave consequences to the people of this country, should war come.
As I have said, I read the recent remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I also read in the Cleveland Plain Dealer an address he made about May last during his visit to the United States. I keep in touch with press reports through the reading room and otherwise; in fact I have looked over five or six hundred newspapers since the war started, and I can tell the minister as regards the money he is spending to convert the people of the United States, that if it is conversion he wants, he is going the wrong way about it. All the money you spend in connection with United States weekly and daily newspapers from coast to coast in regard to this information is wasted. After all is said and done, things are not the same as in the last War. We have failed to understand the commercialization of the press that has occurred in the interval. Often the great dailies in London, New York and other cities sit on the fence and do not take sides because they do not want to be unpopular. We have failed to notice the extent to which the great weeklies of this country, who are the backbone of independent thought here, have been driven to the wall in these days of war economic stress. With regard to most of this

material that is given out about the war, I would not call it information at all. Would any historian take the views expressed by the parliamentary assistant the other day.
I do not wish to delay the Prime Minister's estimates, but I do not see how the parliamentary assistant can hope to make a success of this branch at this late stage of the war, when three or four other ministers have failed with it, and when the corresponding organizations in England and the United States are continually in hot water. I hope that during the recess of parliament the whole department will be abolished. Let the press do all this work and get its information about the war from the army, the navy and the air force; let it fulfil its function, as it has since time immemorial, in peace and war alike, and transmit the information to the citizens of this country.

Perhaps I should reply to one or two points which have been raised. First, I find that I misinformed the committee in regard to the matter of income tax, which was raised some time ago. The situation is that two members of the staff of fourteen in the United States are residents of that country and pay income tax there. One member of the staff was an employee of the British government when taken over by the board, and for some technical reason he may not be liable to tax in the United States. ' The other eleven members of the staff pay Canadian income tax on salary and allowances, so that a good deal of the discussion we had previously might have been obviated if I could have given the leader of the opposition this information, which of course fortifies my position very greatly in regard to the salaries of the employees in the United States.
The hon. member for Lake Centre asked a question in regard to how some fourteen jobs were ordered by the board and what control was kept over the editorial work done on them. In those cases the work was actually done for the board by people expert in that work; the board assumed full responsibility for it; there was complete control throughout, and a small fee was paid for the services rendered.
In reply to the hon. member for Broadview, I can only say that his understanding of the situation with respect to information in Great Britain is not up to date. By all accounts the present minister is making an extraordinary success of his job. The debates in the House of Commons, which I have followed and which I have in my hand, are full of compliments to a minister who is doing a difficult job and doing it exceedingly

well. Far from the flood of leaflets over Germany being stopped, it has been multiplied almost a thousand-fold, and is known to do exceedingly good work. The work of the ministry of information in England is more appreciated to-day than it has been at any stage of the war.

speechtext:
I am not going to delay the committee for very long, either, but I want to compliment the parliamentary assistant upon his presentation in behalf of the wartime information board1. When the question of appointing assistants to the various ministers was brought up, the members of this group felt that there was absolute necessity for this step being taken, and I think the way in which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is handling the matter before the committee this afternoon fully justifies his appointment.
Much could be said on the subject now under consideration. The hon. member for Broadview emphasizes the fact that the dissemination of information to the public is largely the business of the press. My personal observation is that if what we have been getting in the press for the past three or four years is any indication as to their ability to educate the public, then I am all for setting up some other agency which will see to it that the public gets all the facts in respect of any matter requiring publicity. I read all sections of the press. I have heard discussions in the house of matters of which we have intimate knowledge, and one would not recognize those discussions as they are given to the public through the medium of the press. If the press is to retain the confidence of the public and a place in the future of our country, then regard will have to be had to many sections of it, to see that it gives the public frankly and without any reservation the facts disclosed, so that public opinion may be moulded in accordance with actual conditions.
Replying to the hon. member for York-Sunbury, the parliamentary assistant said
that the main function of the wartime information board was to send propaganda to the people of the United States. I believe such an observation would be misleading to the public. To-day the average person associates propaganda with totalitarian countries. Those countries have used the word "propaganda" to the world at large in order to sell something' to the people which actually did not exist. They have tried to build their machines into machines representing freedom and democracy, so that propaganda in the mind of the average man leaves the impression that we are trying to sell him something phony.
In my opinion the main function of the wartime information board is to tell the people of the United States the truth about what is going on in Canada, so that we may be able to get together on a basis of mutual understanding of what is taking place. I believe the wartime information board is and has been performing a useful service in this time of war.
Then, I have kept in close touch with what has been done by the national film board. I believe the chairman of that board, Mr. Grierson, is doing an important job in an important educational field. In my view visual education is the greatest medium of educating the public. I have seen many of the films produced by the film board since the outbreak of war. They have endeavoured to inform all the provinces in Canada of what is actually taking place, in order that Canadians may see each other in their respective provinces and in their various endeavours, so that the economic operations of all might be carried on more effectively. I believe I am speaking on behalf of this group when I compliment the national film board upon the job it is doing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should like to make a few comments following the explanations by the parliamentary assistant. My observations will deal more particularly with my experiences on my recent trip to the United States. I believe what I learned at that time should be brought to the attention of the Prime Minister, with a view to having certain changes made which in my opinion would materially improve our relations with the United States.
The parliamentary assistant made a comparison between expenditures in Canada and those in Great Britain and the United States. I fail to see the significance of such comparisons. In the matter of propaganda, a process which to-day assumes greater proportions than ever before, there are three phases. The first is that of the home front; the second concerns



War Appropriation-External Affairs
friendly or allied nations and, so far as Canada is concerned particularly concerns the United States of America. The third phase is that of operations by way of propaganda directed against the enemy. In other words information may be divided into two groups, one offensive and the other defensive. The operations of the wartime information board in Canada are not of the offensive type, in that they are not primarily directed against the enemy, whereas Great Britain and the United States have to build up a counter-propaganda system against axis nations. We in Canada have not had to do that to any extent, but Great Britain must answer the propaganda of the enemy nations. That accounts in large measure for the difference in the expenditures made by information boards in England and in Canada.
I believe there is no more important branch than the wTartime information board. Recent history has shown that the failure to answer enemy propaganda in allied countries, however implausible that propaganda may be, may result in dangerous divisions taking place. What Canada needs more than ever to-day is direct and truthful propaganda used as an antidote against some of the false propaganda being circulated.
If I remember correctly, the Prime Minister pointed out this afternoon that the United States has not at all times had a full appreciation of Canada's constitutional position. I feel, too, that she does not appreciate the many facets of the war effort of this dominion. There is nothing more important to-day than our relationship with the United States, owing to the fact that she is a great allied nation and our nearest neighbour. Our relations must be based upon an appreciation of what each nation is doing, and to that end the people of the United States should be told what Canada is doing in the war. ,
In Canada we hear every day what is being done in the United States. That information comes to us over the radio, in the newspapers and in the magazines published in the United States. However, in the short time I was there I found there were Americans in public life who had insufficient knowledge of the fact that last year this parliament made provision for a billion-dollar transfer of goods to Great Britain-the so-called gift. What is more, they have little or no knowledge of the billion-dollar mutual aid bill recently passed in the house. While the parliamentary assistant has said much regarding the improvement in conditions in the United States, so far as war-time information is concerned, I say there is plenty of room for a great improvement and for a wider dissemination of

news regarding our war contribution. A moment ago my hon. friend mentioned the number of press references that had been made, I believe it was something like four hundred in the last-

I know my hon. friend will not mind my interrupting him, because it is only a matter of having the right information. He must recall that until the United States was actually in the war there was in the United States a strong feeling against any attempt on the part of Canada to influence the people in a way which might be held to be political, namely, to make from Canada by way of propaganda an effort to bring the United States into the war. It was held the reactions might be serious. I am justified in saying that I was asked by the highest authority in the United States to see that great care was taken to avoid making

any move by which it could be said that the government of Canada was trying to influence public opinion in the United States with a view to having the United States brought into the war against its will. All of that had to be carefully considered before Canada was justified in appointing any board for the purpose of distributing information in the United States with regard to the war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
All that the Prime Minister has said would apply prior to December, 1941, prior to Pearl Harbor, but after that date there was a hiatus until October, 1942, during which period little information was given to the people of the United States. It was only in October, 1942, following the pressure the Prime Minister says he received from editors and, I would submit, from members of this opposition also, that there was an extension of facilities in the United States. While we in Canada have been able to learn what the United States effort is, I repeat that in the United States there is not the knowledge of our war effort that there should be.
I think the limitation upon holding conventions in and tourist traffic in Canada should be removed. The matter of exchange is not so important to-day as it was at the time tourist traffic was almost excluded from this country. The United States and Canada are working together under mutual aid schemes and lend-lease, and the need for the restriction of tourist traffic is not as great as it was previously. There is nothing so beneficial to the relationship between countries, especially countries lying side by side, as the interchange of ideas consequent on the visit of tourists. I submit that something should be done to remove the present almost impregnable wall that exists in Canada against visits of United States tourists.

speechtext: Give them more gasoline.

The hon. member for Davenport suggests that consideration should be given to granting an extra allowance of gasoline to tourists. I would suggest also that public speakers from Canada should be permitted and encouraged to go to the United States. At one time there was a speakers' bureau which arranged for the payment, in whole or in part, of expenses of speakers going to the United States. I understand that this has been done away with, but I speak subject to correction. In the recent visit to the United States of some members of this house we found that the people there are anxious to know about Canada and about our war effort. I submit that there would be no better way of doing this than to remove the unnecessary financial regulations in regard to tourist traffic
72537-299$
and to encourage the holding of conventions in Canada and the arranging for speakers from Canada to go to the United States. I make these suggestions because I believe there is nothing so necessary to-day as the dissemination in the United States of selectve information, truthful information and, finally, the repetition of the information that is being distributed. This must be done in order to refute and combat misinformation which breeds easily and is a productive source of difficulty as between nations.
There are other observations I intended to make, one of which has to do with our soldiers overseas. To-day they are not permitted to receive newspapers. I realize that for a time this was necessary, but I contend that the best way the soldier overseas can be prevented from becoming homesick is to be made aware of what is happening on the home front. There should be a restoration to him of the right to secure Canadian newspapers. If that cannot be done, the wartime information board should establish a weekly or monthly publication which would set out what is happening in Canada. The parliamentary assistant, who has displayed the essence of courtesy in the way in which he has answered questions to-day, has sent me over a copy of "Canadian Affairs". This is a new pamphlet published for the Canadian army overseas by the wartime information board. It is entitled "Canada in the Fourth Year of War", by B. K. Sandwell, and I am going to refer to it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
