subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does it edit the news?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No, it does not edit it. The news is sent down by the agencies over their wires to their correspondents in the United States, the Associated Press and the United Press, and it gets into the United States newspapers through the news service giving it distribution. The services of the wartime information board are in facilitating the flow of news at every point. It does not have anything to do with the collection of news or the direct distribution of news. It is a service that it is rendering, facilitating the flow of the news.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Then we are down to this. So far as the wartime information board is concerned, in the United States it runs a service in cooperation with the regular press services by directing the attention of the United States newspapers to available information.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

I have in my hands the pamphlet, "Canadian Affairs", which the parliamentary assistant says is information for the troops. What does the pamphlet itself say? Articles which appear in "Canadian Affairs" should be regarded as expressing the views of the individual Canadians who write them. These are not necessarily the views of the Department of National Defence, the wartime information board, or any other government authority.
(Mr. Diefonbaker.]

speechtext:
In the committee on radio broadcasting, which brought in its report at the end of the last session, some time was taken up in considering the question of the dissemination and perhaps the channelling of news and information from various departments of government. The parliamentary assistant was a member of that committee and took an active part in its work. He will recall, as will other members who took part in the committee, that evidence was adduced there indicating that some change was in the mind of the government looking to a more effective channelling of information coming from various governmental departments to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. What I wish to refer to is not related to press publication but rather to the radio.
There was evidence before the committee on one or two occasions that there was no real coordination in regard to information from various government sources-the wartime prices and trade board, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Agriculture and other departments-but that
these departments, by a more or less hit-or-miss method, were competing, or at least that there was possibility that they might compete, for time on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation network. Some intimation was also given by those who gave evidence that the government had in mind at that time extending the work of the interdepartmental committee which was set up, I believe, under the chairmanship of the Hon. T. C. Davis, who was later appointed as Australian minister. That interdepartmental committee's workings have been spoken of from time to time in the committee itself, and I was wondering if the hon. gentleman could tell us whether it was working in conjunction with the wartime information board, which had been set up since the radio committee had brought in its findings.
May I quote from the Ottawa Journal of April 3 of this year, from an article under the title, "John Grierson defends work of war information board". At one stage of his observations he states:
Each department of government had its own information service issuing material to the public. WJ.B. is not immediately concerned with these services, but has the duty of seeing to it that, in consultation with the departmental officers concerned, wastage of effort is kept within limits, campaigns are related and contradictions avoided.
That seems to put the matter on all fours with what was discussed in the radio committee at the last session of the house. I was wondering if the parliamentary assistant could give some information concerning the relationship between the wartime information board's activities and those of the interdepartmental committee, or whether the wartime information board has taken over the work of that committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

The question of coordinating the activities of the various information services is kept constantly in mind. There is one committee, the national campaign committee, under the chairmanship of Brigadier James Mess, which deals with the general subject of national campaigns in the broadest sense. It has representation from the various departments concerned. There is also a publicity coordinating committee, which I think is the committee the hon. member has particularly in mind, which was formerly chaired by the Hon. T. C. Davis, and that committee actually, works on the business of coordinating war-time information, whether it be from the various government departments or from the wartime information board. In addition to that, it would be fair to say that since the report of the broadcasting committee, to which the hon. gentleman has referred, there has been

I should like to get an answer from the parliamentary assistant in regard to "Canada at War" and the omission of information from the March, April, May and June issues with respect to the call-up and enlistment of men in the various military districts. This afternoon the parliamentary assistant said he would bring the matter to the attention of the board. That is not enough. Parliament has a right to know what should be in that booklet, and an explanation is due. The parliamentary assistant said that the reason why it was omitted was that parliament was in session. I accept that explanation. Then the question was asked whether he would give an assurance that this information would be furnished in issues following the prorogation of parliament, and the answer was that the matter would be brought to the attention of the board. The omission of this item has been the subject of considerable editorial comment and is a matter of interest to people everywhere. It gives them a picture from month to month of what Canada is doing in regard to manpower in all parts of the dominion. It makes for competition between districts and arouses, on the part of those districts which are contributing men, that enthusiasm which enables them to maintain the record of leading Canada in recruiting. During recent months, when a certain military district was ahead, 
the people resident in that district and the newspapers were very proud of the fact that they were leading the dominion. Competition is engendered as a result of furnishing that information, which cannot be secured in any other way. If we want the man-power, this is one way in which districts would vie with one another in a competitive play to head the dominion. I ask for some assurance that this be re-included in "Canada at War". It is not information which by any stretch of the imagination can do any harm to this nation. It was given for months. I ask the parliamentary assistant to place before the people the situation. Let us know w'hy it has been omitted and when it will be restored.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps I should have explained at greater length how "Canadian Affairs" originated, but I thought I had taken up enough of the time of the committee. There are two publications issued by the British army, "Current Affairs" and "War". They are issued to all officers and, I think, a considerable number of other ranks in the British army as well as in the Canadian forces. They are extraordinarily useful publications, and by General McNaughton and others it was thought desirable that we should supplement these publications with another of our own. Accordingly "Canadian Affairs" was decided upon, as it states, to fill a long-felt want. If my hon. friend is familiar with the other publications he will see that the set-up of this pamphlet is very similar to that of the other two. I think reference to the other
publications will indicate that everything about this pamphlet is similar to them. The other publications are written in part by individuals, in the same way, and the board issuing them disclaims any responsibility for the views expressed. That is in order that they may not become totally colourless, and it indicates that they carry no official sanction. AYith regard to reprinting, the wartime information board has been requested for permission to reprint articles from this publication on at least two occasions, both in Great Britain; once by a newspaper and once by one of the British army publications, and that permission was given instantly. The qualification with regard to reprinting I should think appears on every publication issued for the army. There is no objection to the material being used, provided some control is kept over its use, and that is one reason for putting in that restriction. It is also intended to protect those who are asked to contribute their services for these purposes. The Prime Minister has already read to the committee the appreciation of the first number from General McNaughton. I should think the committee, and everyone else, would be completely satisfied that this was a desirable publication issued in the interests of our soldiers overseas definitely to keep them better informed and properly safeguarded in every way. It was just the kind of thing that General McNaughton wanted, and that he said in his telegram he wanted.

I know those British publications, and they do not contain any of the political references this booklet contains. I will read one of them, and I would ask the committee whether or not it contains information objectively given for the benefit of the troops overseas. Here is one quotation:
High Taxation Here to Stay
The social effects of this steeply graduated taxation will be incalculable. Only a small fraction of them is now visible, because taxpayers have not yet adjusted their style of living to their new circumstances.
And a little later on:
Any expectation that this rate of taxation can be much lessened after the war is fast disappearing, as it comes to be realized that Canada cannot avoid sharing in the burden of putting Europe and the orient on their feet again, and as political parties vie with one another in their promises of legislation for social betterment at home. It cannot be said that there is any serious resentment about these changes, which are accepted as inevitable and as likely in the long run to be beneficial to the nation; the chief concern of the "successful" classes is to preserve some area of opportunity for private enterprise.
Then he goes on to refer to the purpose of continuing taxation at its present level, as



War Appropriation-External Affairs
against the demands of the socialists for the elimination of the whole profit motive from commerce and industry. There are many such quotations in the book.
I think that must have been written by a member of the Progressive Conservative party.
It is written by Mr. Sandwell.
We ought to have an explanation why political propaganda like that is put out in the guise of objective information to the army.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that it is not political propaganda. What is the sense of trying to create the impression that it is political propaganda? It is nothing of the kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Carried.

No. I have listened with great interest this afternoon to the lucid explanations given by the parliamentary assistant to the Prime Minister. One thing which surprised me was his statement that Mr. Grierson had only one salary. I remember the time when Mr. Grierson received only $6,000 from the film board, but it has now jumped to $10,000. Therefore, if he has only one salary, then it is a salary with a big belly, meaning by that that instead of having a salary of only $6,000 a year, he has one of $10,000. Well, I have no objection to that; but the whole story should be told. He is there, and he looks after the film board, a very fine institution. Then, we realize the information board is not such a fine institution, and I think a distinction should be made between them. The information board does not inform people as they should be informed about everything.
In the first place, French-speaking people in this country should be informed about English-speaking people, and vice versa, so that we may come to an understanding. But nothing of that sort is done. What is the use of keeping an information board when there is an information branch in each department? There is one in the Department of Munitions and Supply and also one in the Department of Labour. Why do we have this fifth wheel called the information board? I am not saying that to be critical. I remember distinctly that the matter of information was covered by the Department of National War Services, before that department was entrusted to the hon. member who is now minister of that department. As soon as he was sworn in, it was taken away from that department, and placed
fMr. Diefenbaker.]
under the Prime Minister. Why was such a change made? I wonder if the hon. member who is now parliamentary assistant has explained why the information board has been taken away from the Minister of National War Services, and put into the hands of the Prime Minister. I might speak again to-night as the defender of widows and orphans, but in this respect the orphan is the Minister of National War Services who has been put in charge of a department with nothing in it, except the scissors of censorship. That is the way I take it.
I appreciate that the Minister of National War Services, who has nothing to do in his department except look after Mr. Oliver Mowat Biggar's office, would have much more time to look after information than would the Prime Minister, who is a very busy man. Who would expect the Prime Minister to have the time to read all these publications? I am sure he was grateful to the hon. member for Lake Centre when he read from the publication to the committee to-night. Do you think, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister of Canada, the busiest man in the country, has time to read all these publications? Then, why was it not put under a gentleman of leisure, a minister of leisure, who has very little to do in his department, and would have the time to scrutinize the whole thing? This could be done simply, and in good order.
I have no grudge against anyone. I think Mr. Grierson is a fine fellow. But why should we always go to an outsider when we want something done in Canada? When it came to the film board we took Mr. Grierson, who came from Scotland. And he was not the only Scotsman. For radio we have Doctor Thomson, who comes from Scotland. For reconstruction we have James of McGill, from England. All these outsiders come to this country to teach Canadians what they shall do in the post-war era, and what they should do during the war. Are there not any Canadians who could do it? More than that, these outsiders are taken into the employ of the government because of the deep religious feeling held by His Majesty's Loyal Opposition for all outsiders. It is the impression of the government that so long as they hire the services of outsiders the opposition will accept them and give them their kotows in true Japanese fashion. They will put their noses together in a long embrace. The government goes to these outsiders, people coming from the British isles, and has them take these key positions in Canada so that every time something is done they may say, "Well, it was that Englishman who did it", or that Scotsman who did it, or that Irishman. And then the opposition will make kotows to them.

War Appropriation-External Affairs
That is all very well. But if the opposition *were not so ready to fill these boards with outsiders, it would be better for the country, and we would have Canadians in charge of important matters, matters which at the present time are run by outsiders. I do not object to Grierson as Grierson, but I do object to Grierson as an outsider coming to teach us. I object to Doctor Thomson for the same reason. And I object to James of McGill on the same grounds. I object to the fact that these people come out to teach the bloated colonials in Canada what they have to do.
Then, with regard to the film board, we know a great many pictures have been taken of our Prime Minister. At one time I said that Mr. Grierson had so many pictures of the Prime Minister that I was sure the exposures were as numerous as the sands of the seas and the stars in the sky. How many pictures does he have that are still undeveloped? How many are there in the vaults of the film board? They are fine pictures the country should see and we should like to see, but we have not yet had the privilege of seeing them. It seems to me that for these reasons we should not be excessive in our praise, and we should get some information on the pictorial side of the matter.
I have something else in mind. How much money has been spent for McKenna, for instance? McKenna is the man who was a correspondent of a United States paper in the press gallery. What were the expenditures for trips to New York, trips to everywhere, trips to nowhere? And what about payments to Paul Reading, who wears out I do not know how many pairs of boot soles walking in the corridors of this house. There are Paul Reading and McKenna, and how many others? We see them around the corridors all the time; that is, all the time they are in Ottawa. How much money has been paid to them for travelling expenses? Instead of putting forth the theory about what should be done and what should not be done in the way of propaganda, we should first know what it costs. That is the first question that should be asked by the opposition. Why did the opposition not ask how much Paul Reading had received for travelling expenses, living expenses, and this and that? How much money did McKenna get? How much money did he pass over to other journalists for travelling expenses? These would be good things to know. We should have the dollars and cents. I wonder if the Prime Minister has been informed of all these details.
Why should the wartime information board be treated as a kind of holy of holies about
72537-300i
which we cannot get any information when we ask about the regulations and the censorship? We should be told about the regulations and about the censorship, or at least about the censorship regulations. How is it that these people can publish anything, while other papers have not the same right? What is the use of having a wartime information board if it does not inform the Canadian people? The Canadian people are entitled to the truth; that is the kind of news they should get. There are some journalists who are ready -or Reading-to go along with that kind of thing, but there are others who are honest and who realize that when they represent the press they fulfil a sacred duty to the public. Very often important news has been hidden from the public, news that should1 have been given to the public in order to inspire confidence in the government. Sometimes people lose confidence in the government because of the wrong this has done in connection with supplying news to the Canadian people.
Canadians have a right to expect true and reliable information from the papers to which they have subscribed. This public institution, the wartime information board, is not supported directly by the Canadian people, because there are no subscribers to the board such as there are to newspapers, but on the other hand the expenses come out of the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers and they are entitled to have value for the taxes they pay to support the board. They have a right to know what the expenses of this board are; what expenses are being paid to McKenna, whom I mentioned, and Reading and many others. We see them in the corridors of the house trying to check the news and trying to create false propaganda. I know whereof I speak.
All this is said in the best possible spirit and in order that the wartime information board may serve a definite purpose. There is a man in Canada who has done more to supply the public with information than any government institution. I refer to Emile Vaillancourt of Montreal. He has supplied the press with all sorts of information about all sorts of things. I read to the house the letter which he wrote last year to Winston Churchill, and the Prime Minister said it was a good letter in spite of the protests of the then leader of the opposition who did not listen long enough to see how much to the point it was. How is it that the government has not asked Emile Vaillancourt, not to join the board but to be the head of the board? He is a most gifted man; he knows a great deal more about publicity and Canadian

history than Philippe Brais. Mr. Brais may know something about the civil code and statutory procedure, enactments and things like that, but he is not at all cultured. But here is a man who is cultured ; here is a man who is public spirited; here is a man who is fully qualified to be the head of this institution and to make a success of it. But he is left aside; he is left in the shade, perhaps because he is too independent. It does not mean that he is not a good Canadian; he is a first-class Canadian. The testimonial that was given to him by the Prime Minister in this chamber is something that cannot be forgotten. Among the best things that have come from the pens of Canadians is this letter to Churchill. But he has done more than that. He has led public discussions over the radio and has had them printed at his own expense and distributed to hon. members. How is it that a man so well gifted, who has done so much at his own expense, is not asked to -lead and to make a success of this board? He would make English-speaking Canadians understand that there are some French-speaking Canadians who can do as well as any men imported into the country.
We are all Canadians. I am not prejudiced; I am not biased, but in this case I think Emile Yaillancourt is the best man we could have had. I am sure that the Prime Minister, his parliamentary assistant and all the members of the committee appreciate the excellent work that has been done by Emile Vaillancourt. During war time there is a need to unite Canada, instead of dividing it for the benefit of a few people and to the detriment of the community at large.
Would the Prime Minister be good enough to place my name on the mailing list for "Canadian Affairs"?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I shall direct the attention of the board to my hon. friend's request.
It is a public document published by the wartime information board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not interfered with the board or its work, and I prefer to maintain that attitude. I shall be glad to refer my hon. friend's request to the board, and I am sure they will be happy to meet it.
I should like to say a word in regard to one remark made by the hon. member for Temis-couata. He asked why it was that the information board was placed under the president of the council immediately after the Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaFleche) had been appointed, the implica-

tion being that this was done because the Minister of National War Services happened to be a French Canadian. That is as I understood the impression the hon. gentleman was seeking to leave. He suggested that as soon as the minister had taken over this portfolio, the board was transferred from his responsibility to that of the president of the council. I hope I am not misconstruing what my hon. friend had in mind and intended to convey.
I should like to make clear to the committee the reason why the board was placed under the president of the council. Mr. Yining was asked to prepare a report for the government on the whole question of war information and the best way of facilitating the distribution of information. He recommended that the board should be under the president of the council rather than any other minister in order that interdepartmental cooperation might be more effectively obtained. This was not likely to be the case to the same degree if the board remained under any one other particular minister. That recommendation was made while an English-speaking minister was at the head of the Department of National War Services and before the present minister took office. It is only fair that these facts should be made perfectly clear.

I did not want to convey the impression that I was complaining because the wartime information board had been taken from the Department of National War Services at the time of the appointment of the present minister because he was a French Canadian. That was not the question at all. What I said was that as soon as the gentleman was sworn in, the board was turned out. I thank the Prime Minister for his explanation, but I did not mention either the race or religion of the present Minister of National War Services when I made my statement.

Reference has been made to the faot that there are information boards or publicity offices in a number of the ministries and in branches of the armed services. I wonder if we might have information as to just what other ministries maintain offices of this kind, and to what extent the wartime information board serves to coordinate the work done by these other offices, or whether there is no coordination between these separate offices and the wartime information board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The material required to answer that question has already been given in the return which was brought down to the house some time ago. So far as I know, the situation has not changed since. I will refer the hon. member for York South to the return if I may, on the adjournment.

War Appropriation-External Affairs
I should like the parliamentary assistant to be kind enough to tell us how much money was paid for travelling expenses, living allowance, and all that, to Mr. McKenna and Mr. Reading.
May I ask if the return to which the parliamentary assistant referred touched on the question of coordination between the different publicity offices and the wartime information board.

I am sorry; it just gives factual information about the number of press representatives in the various departments of the government. I have already said something at the beginning of the sitting to-night on the question of coordination. There is every effort made at coordination, and that coordination is very close with the public relations officers of the board. Mr. J. W. G. Clark, director of public relations of the department of defence works closely with the wartime information board, and the same is true of the other departments. In addition, there are, as I mentioned before, a number of provisions which are specially designed to accomplish what my hon. friend has in mind.
In reply to the question of the hon. member for Temiscouata, return No. 176, which was brought down in the house on March 2, 1943, discloses that no expenses were paid to Mt. McKenna and none to Mr. Reading since the organization of the board. I am informed that since that date Mr. McKenna has had one trip to the United States to see people with whom he has to deal there and those in charge of the distribution of foreign news going to the United States, and that Mr. Reading has had no travelling expenses since then whatsoever.
How much was paid to Mr. McKenna for his travelling expenses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not that information here.
Will the hon. gentleman please give it to me later?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
Thank you.

I think there should be some little correction made of an impression which the hon. member for Temiscouata may have left, though I do not know that I am the man to make the correction. The hon. member seemed particularly vociferous in his condemnation of the government for bringing in from outside this country men of expert knowledge. I do not know all the men that he mentioned, but he did mention Doctor Thomson, who to-day is the managing director
of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the impression one might get from the hon. member's remarks is that the government sent over to Scotland for Doctor Thomson, which of course, is not the case. I think with all due respect for Doctor Thomson that should be made perfectly plain. I happened to be a member of the radio committee of last year and I think, if the evidence is examined together with the reports of that committee, it will be found that we were particularly anxious that should there be a change in the managing directorship of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the position should be filled by someone from Canada. I am not attempting to come to the assistance of the government in saying this, but the fact is that Doctor Thomson was released from ithe university of Saskatchewan, I believe at the request of the government, in order that he might assume the duties of managing-director of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for this year. He was not imported for that job.
While I am on my feet I should like 'to say that there is a principle involved that was well stated by the hon. member for Temiscouata. It does seem that very often we import what we may regard as experts, while perhaps many experts in our own midst leave us to work in other countries, particularly in the country to the south, where the fields may appear to be greener. I see no reason why Canada should be one whit behind any other nation in the world in producing experts in every possible field of modern civilization. I have mentioned before, and I think I should mention it again now, that the Prime Minister is in his seat, that we have doctors of philosophy in the various sciences working in our civil service to-day for wages that are less than what is paid to a grade 3 stenographer. That should not be so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe that for some little time I have been remiss in my duty. I allowed the hon. member for Temiscouata to mention persons born outside Canada. That was my mistake, and I shall be compelled from now on to keep speakers to the item before the Chair.

Very well, Mr. Chairman. I have always regarded you as being fair, and I think you are fair now. Your point is well taken, but I am of the opinion that the hon. member for Temiscouata must not get away with anything more than any other-private member of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I made it very plain that some part of his discussion was out of order, and that it was my mistake in not

War Appropriation-External Affairs
calling him to order. I believe it is the sentiment of ninety-mine per cent of the committee that we should stay within the orbit of the item we are discussing.
Mr. H'ANSELL: Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
Now may I get back to the wartime information board. I have no fault to find with the board, but I want to make this observation. The Prime Minister took exception to a remark a little while ago from the official opposition in regard to political propaganda. I do not know that that was precisely the term used. I am not going to say that the wartime information board is used for political propaganda, but I make this observation, that there can hardly be a piece of literature issued by the wartime information board on what is being done in Canada to-day without carrying with it a psychological impression that the Liberal government is doing a good job. "Canada at War" comes out once a month and I like to read it; I get a lot of information from it. But anyone reading that publication is	apt	to saythat it	is	simply a build-up for	the	presentgovernment. And it is. I am not saying that it	is	intentionally so, but	the	fact isthat it	is,	and the result is that	the	department has all the advantage that this publication gives.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
A corrective, so far as that is concerned, if any be needed, is furnished in full measure by what appears in some organs of the press. I rose to comment upon one matter mentioned, namely, with respect to certain persons holding positions in the country, the suggestion made being that such positions are necessarily to be reserved for persons born in Canada. I am as strong a Canadian as anyone in this house, but I should be very sorry if the day ever came when we decided to make it even an indirect condition that a person, in order to hold a high position in Canada, must necessarily have been born in this country. I think of the positions of hon. members in this house. There is no more honourable position in Canada than that of member of parliament. When I look diagonally opposite I see a good many gentlemen who would not be in this House of Commons to-day, if the people had not sent them here, notwithstanding the fact that they were not born in Canada. It is one of the glories of this country that any man may come to Canada and feel that he has a chance to help to serve not only the people of Canada, but if he has the ability, mankind itself, men and women of all classes and creeds and countries. I do not forget that (The Chairman.]
the great leader of the Conservative party, the first Prime Minister of this country, a man whom all of us honour, irrespective of party, wms from the old country; I do not forget either that he was a Scotsman. When you find gentlemen in high positions and you are told at the same time that they come from Scotland, you may feel pretty sure that the appointment is a fairly good one.

I do not know why the Prime Minister was facing me all the time, because I did not make the charge; it was the hon. member for Temiscouata who made it. I rose to say just about what the Prime Minister has said, in defence of Doctor Thomson, a man already in Canada. However, I do not mind the Prime Minister looking this way once in a while.
In regard to the publication "Canadian Affairs", can the parliamentary assistant say how many copies have been distributed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The last issue was 23,000. They are printed in England by the wartime information- board for the Department of National Defence.
What is the cost of that issue?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know the cost. It is charged to the Department of National Defence.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Privy Council.
Advisory committee on reconstruction, $47,250.

This is a vote for the advisory committee on reconstruction. Most hon. members are acquainted with what the parliamentary committee on reconstruction and rehabilitation is doing. It has an able chairman and an able vice-chairman, both of whom deserve a good deal of credit. But what is this advisory committee doing? I have been a member of the parliamentary committee and we have had some of the members of the advisory committee before us, but I do not know what they are doing. The war may be over at any time, and I hope it is; but if the war ended to-morrow, just what plans and specifications are ready to give men jobs? We have been talking now for the last four hours about publicity. Publicity is very necessary, I admit, in the conduct of government, but the providing of jobs when the war is over is infinitely more important. We shall get a good deal of

War Appropriation-External Affairs
unfavourable publicity after the war if there are many thouands of men unemployed as there were after the last war.
There is a multitude of opportunities to provide jobs. I know of a multitude myself, but I will not enumerate them. However, let me give one small project as a sample of what can be done, and what I believe should be done, if this advisory committee is the one that is to prepare for the provision of jobs. If it is to submit plans and specifications to provide jobs, it ought to be preparing right now. I do not know that much has been done so far. I have read speeches by members of the committee who are doing good work in their way, but we have to go much farther than that. We have to get together a large number of plans and specifications of jobs to which men can be directed immediately the war is over, or we shall find ourselves in the same boat as we did after the last war.
I was closely associated with business after the last war, and I know that business closed up tight and men did not get jobs. I had so much to do with jobs that perhaps I talk about this subject more than I should, but one cannot overemphasize the importance of providing work, and the men cannot get it by talk but by careful preparation. They cannot be paid for the work they do by talk but by money, and to be paid money they have to render some service in return.
Recently there was an article in the newspapers about the riding represented by my leader, the riding of Peel, where somebody in the towm of Brampton had given to the press a plan for a proposed diversion of a small creek running through the town. It is called Etobicoke river. North of that town the watershed1 of the river is very small, about twenty-five square miles, but to give an indication of what a small watershed like that can do if there should be a cloudburst or a heavy three-day rain, the amount of water that would fall on it could be 160,000,000 cubic feet. That quantity of water rushing through the town would wipe the main street off the map. They have had severe floods there beginning away back in 1878 and down through the years, in 1909, 1929, and last year again, 1942, and the big floods have averaged from $80,000 to $100,000 of damage each time. The whole work on that river to flood-proof it could be done for $100,000. That is one small project. I would ask the Prime Minister courteously to direct this committee, for which this money is being voted, to inform members of parliament and the country what they are doing, and I would ask him to request them in the kindest way to provide plans and specifications for jobs to which many thousands of men could1 be sent to earn an honest dollar when the war ends.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This committee was
appointed by order in council P.C. 609 in January, 1943. It is working with sub-committees, a number of which have made reports. It is hoped that all the reports in the course of preparation will be in, in the month of August or September, and they will be made available as soon as it is in the public interest to give them. There are other committees working on the subject of reconstruction-the committee on rehabilitation and demobilization, the advisory committee on economic policy, the Canadian section of the joint economic board, in addition to the three parliamentary committees. They are all working and are bringing their work to the point where it will be possible for some agency to draw up the plans and specifications to which my hon. friend lias referred.
Are there prepared plans and specifications for a single specific job? Can the hon. member name one solitary job that everything is prepared for?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes; a number of specific jobs have been prepared. A great many are under consideration. There is a sub-committee of the advisory committee on reconstruction, on post-war construction projects. The chairman is Mr. K. M. Cameron, chief engineer of the Department of Public Works, and that committee has made an interim report, I understand, and will make a further report at an early date.
Can the hon. member name one job?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: A survey of the whole country.

Yes; but have they named a single place in this country for which blueprints, plans and specifications have been prepared, to which men can be sent immediately the war closes, as soon as material can get on that job?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think they
have gone as far as my hon. friend would want on that, because the war is not over yet, but I think they are at the stage where they have considered in one way or another a very large number of projects plus a whole system of dealing with specific jobs, and I hope the wish of my hon. friend will be met by the progress that is being made.

I hope so.

speechtext: I hope it is not.

speechtext: The point raised by the horn, member for Lethbridge is under constant consideration by the advisory committee on economic policy.

I remember that a long time ago, about nine years ago, I was campaigning in Ontario-this is by way of comparison-and I was talking with a friend of mine, who by the way is Billy Gordon, now a minister in the Ontario government. I said " Billy, here in Ontario are there people who work on the roads at election time?" He said, " Oh, yes." This was in 1934. I went along the road. The weather was fine; the road was well paved, one of the finest between Wallaceburg and Chatham. At one corner I saw an elevation about one hundred feet from the road. There were people standing there who were clustered as thick as ants. They had shovels and picks in their hands to demolish a little hill, and they were so numerous that they could not wield their shovels or picks for fear of hitting each other. They were too numerous to work. It reminded me of the present situation in Ottawa. What do we want now for reconstruction and planning for the future? We w7ant order at the present time. If we have not order now, what shall we have after the war? We shall have disorder. The only way to have order is to reduce by one half the number of civil servants, and then it will be possible for the others to work. The minister mentioned
that the work is expected to be completed within eight months. Does he mean it will be finished in the spring, eight months from now?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We shall now proceed to the Department of National War Services. Two of the ministers whose items were mentioned last night are unavoidably absent to-night.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Departmental administration, $91,335.
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services): As explained by the Minister of Pensions and National Health, I come on with the consent of this honourable house because other gentlemen are not prepared at the moment. May I begin by saying that should we be fortunate enough to get down to censorship, I would not propose going into that matter now because there are some questions from the loyal opposition which I wish to satisfy.
There is a decrease of $9,165 as compared with last year. That is made up of a decrease in salaries of $11,000 odd. What we ask for this year is: salaries, $53,895; travelling expenses remain at $6,000; printing and stationery at $20,000, and miscellaneous at $5,000. These figures remain the same as they were last year. The difference is to be found in a decrease in salaries, with slight increases in some very small items to arrive at $9,165 net decrease.	[DOT]

Most of the other ministers made a general statement as to the work of their departments. Will the minister do likewise?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I had thought of that, and I made inquiries and was advised by friends that it would be better perhaps if I waited until questions came up in connection with each vote. I come prepared as best I can .tonight to do so. I have no general statement to make to-night, but I shall do my best to try to explain each vote as we reach it, as has been done in some of the other departments.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
War Appropriation-War Services
War charities division
General	 $	46,000
Auxiliary services	 7,000,000

Has the minister a statement to make with regard to a general national appeal for war charities this year? Will it be continued on the same basis as in previous years? Will the charities included in that appeal be the same as those in other years?
Mr. LaFLECHE: The auxiliary services during the present fiscal year will again be dealt with as they were in the year 1942-43. In regard to a joint appeal, I take it the hon. gentleman refers to the Red Cross?

There are six or seven of them.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I think my hon. friend has in mind the Canadian Legion, Knights of Columbus, Y.M.C.A., Y.W.C.A., the Salvation Army and the Navy League. Those are the six national organizations that have been doing, from very early in the war, what are termed auxiliary services. Fund's were first provided for these purposes by an appeal to the public. A little over a year ago it was decided that these services being necessarily and directly for the members of the armed forces, in the interests of all concerned they should be provided by means of funds voted by this house and paid by the Department of National War Services to each of these six national organizations, and in the current fiscal year the, method adopted last year will be followed again.

The same sum of money to each?
Mr. LaFLECHE: We have provided for $500,000 more in the vote now before the committee than last year, because the number of members of the armed forces has increased very considerably, as all hon. members know. I cannot give the figures, but there is a direct ratio between the number of members of the armed forces and the extent, and therefore the expense, of the auxiliary services. One does not know definitely in advance just how much money will be required, for this very good reason. One or more of the six national organizations known as auxiliary services is assigned the duty of carrying on auxiliary services as the need arises in one of the three defence departments, that is, in connection with the navy, the army or the air force. Then there is an interdepartmental committee upon which the representatives of the armed

forces themselves have a majority of votes. In fact, it is the armed forces that really decide whether it shall be this particular organization or another. Finally, the duty and the honour of serving a particular new requirement is assigned to a particular organization, and that is the beginning of what' turns out to be an expense. The organization charged with that particular duty then prepares and submits a budget. It has all the information which the armed forces can furnish. It knows how many members of the service concerned will be stationed at such and such a point. They submit their budget, and it comes before what is known as the national war services advisory board, upon whose recommendation the Minister of National War Services approves or does not approve, as the case may be, and sometimes questions with a view to getting more information. I am trying to explain that there is an increase of $500,000; it is the amount as best can be estimated in advance to be used for requirements which may arise throughout the year.

That extra half a million dollars is allocated by the minister to some of the six auxiliary services after receiving the advice of the committee to which the minister refers; is that it?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Precisely. The requirement is first stated, and the job is assigned to one of the six organizations by the armed forces committee already mentioned. The chosen organization submits the budget to the national war services advisory board; that board recommends to the minister; it is upon the minister's approval that the money is made available, and of course each one of these organizations must account to the Department of National War Services for the money paid to it.
For fear that I may not have as good an opportunity later on this evening, I should like to express my admiration of this national war services advisory board. I have been to their meetings, I have watched1 them work;
I have seen men there who are known from one end of Canada to the other for their achievements in the business world and in the spheres of charity and philanthropy, and I should like to say publicly how solicitous they are to see that all established requirements for the boys and girls in the armed forces are attended to, and how careful they are with the country's money. What I am particularly pleased about, and I make bold to say, what every hon. member will be happy to know, is that approval was given nearly

War Appropriation-War Services
two months ago to set aside and make available a sum of $250,000, I believe, so that these national organizations, the auxiliary services, could follow Canadian troops, the navy or the air force when they take the offensive. I was a very proud man when I saw in the newspaper to-day that one of these auxiliary services is now in Sicily with our fighting forces.

Could the minister give a break-down showing how much was paid to each one of these six organizations last year, and how much he estimates they will need this year?
Mr. LaFLECHE: With pleasure. The latest figures I have, which I must impress upon hon. members were made up before the final figures were completed for last year, although very nearly correct, I understand, are as follows, representing financing for auxiliary service work:
Canadian Legion	 $1,455,549
Knights of Columbus	 869,951
Salvation Army	 1,080,195
Y.M.C.A	 2.527,154
Y.W.C.A	 335,607
Navy League	 281,119
I might explain that the Y.W.C.A. do not operate on as wide a field as the Y.M.C.A. They are an organization of ladies looking after, particularly, the families of men in camp. They receive them and look after them. I know they were established at Val-cartier camp: my wife went there to see a member of the family, and she told me how nicely these ladies looked after her.
The Navy League, of course, operate in only a few places in Canada. They do a marvellous work for marvellous men-the merchant seamen particularly, as of course, the navy men, and they do not require to be financed in the amounts needed by the other four principal associations.

The Red Cross has not come into this arrangement of the auxiliary services. I believe it declined to do so last year, and it is not yet in. Therefore does the minister anticipate that there will be a national Red Cross appeal in the coming year?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am sure the hon. member for Yale will not mind if I attempt to explain the situation somewhat. The Canadian Red Cross society is not one of the auxiliary services financed from the public treasury, as these other six associations are. There was, I understand, at the time some question of a joint appeal when these associations were raising funds to do auxiliary services work with funds raised by public subscription. I do not
know sufficiently well to say why the Red Cross did not come in, but I have every reason to believe that the Canadian Red Cross society and the other associations are quite happy at the way things are going and quite satisfied with their present status in relation to what I am trying to explain. It is true that this year there was a national campaign for the Red Cross. They set their objective at $10,000,000, and all are glad that they went beyond the mark. We know there is always plenty of good, patriotic work of this kind which can be done if the funds are available. There is rarely too much money either in the church or in charitable or patriotic societies. I would expect, although it is not yet settled, that there will be another public subscription campaign for the Canadian Red Cross society. The dates have not yet been fixed; I am not even sure that they have applied for permission to hold their public campaign, but I take it for granted that they will again request permission to do so. I hope that the Canadian people will as generously support the appeal.

Is it not the fact that the Red Cross cannot receive, by virtue of the Geneva convention or some other provision, grants from government or public funds; that it must be independent?
Mr. LaFLECHE: The hon. member for St. Paul's has correctly stated the attitude and contention of the Canadian Red Cross society. I should like to be able to say definitely whether that contention is in all respects correct. I would rather put it in this way, that it is really a matter which has to do with international relations, if not international law, and I am sure the hon. gentleman will not hold me to an absolutely definite answer one way or the other. The Canadian Red Cross society hold that the fact that they are part of the International Red Cross organization prevents them from being financed by or with government funds. That is the position they take, and I should think there is much to be said for their contention.

I have had a long connection with this charity business, and in the last war things were done differently. About six weeks ago I asked the finance department to give me a statement in regard to the War Charities Act, which was passed in the fall of 1939, I think about a month after war broke out, laying down certain rules and regulations in regard to all charities and auxiliary services. I find that the act is not being carried out. The figures the minister gave to-night are a little at variance With the information I

War Appropriation-War Services
received about six weeks ago. At that time the figure given me was $6,000,000, while for the coming year the minister says the amount will be about $7,000,000, and he has given a list of the charities which are included. The Minister of National Defence appointed a commission to go to England and look into these war services, to ascertain if there was any duplication between the Red Cross, the Y.M.C.A., the Knights of Columbus, the Navy League and so on; I think the I.O.D.E. were in it originally but withdrew after a meeting with the minister.
No doubt these organizations have done a great deal of good work; I am not here to criticize them at all, but I say there is much duplication. The report made by the late lamented leader of this party, Doctor Manion, was a good report, but it was never tabled in this house. Looking over it, I find that some of these organizations are overlapping in their work in England and elsewhere. The minister says these people are well satisfied. Of course they are satisfied; they are getting from this fund far more than they expected. We understood that there was to be one fund, and that the victory loan was to have precedence over all war charities. At the time the Minister of Agriculture was in charge of this department he had a meeting with these bodies, at which he told the Red Cross that was the last year they would be allowed to run their own campaign for the raising of money. The Red Cross has always done very fine work at home and abroad, in peace and war alike; there is no criticism of it or of any of the other fine war charities, but it is up to the government to find out if there is any overlapping. Some of this work which originally was done exclusively by one organization has now been extended so that six or seven different bodies participate in it, and they all seem to have their ways of raising money. Take the one at the foot of the list, with some $200,000. They go to work and raise funds in the city of Montreal; then in Toronto they have a Navy League compaign; then they come along and have a tag day. When the War Charities Act was passed the minister was given power to make rules and regulations which would have almost the force and effect of law, in order that the activities of these organizations might be controlled; yet these charities are appealing to the public for additional funds. The hon. member for Temiscouata was given an answer about a week ago, which appeared in Hansard, in regard to war charities, and I think the figures he obtained are about the same as those which were given by the minister a few moments ago.
tMr. Church.]
I believe further study should be given this matter. After all, $7,000,000 is a great deal of money to be taken from the taxpayers, especially in view of the fact that almost every day of the week they are asked for some donation or other, and almost every Saturday there is some kind of tag day to raise money for war purposes. In addition, I believe the Y.M.C.A. made a public appeal last spring for about $250,000, with advertising on billboards and so on, which must have cost a good deal of money. I should like to mention one other fund which does not cost the state a cent;
I refer to the Toronto Telegram's fund for British w'ar victims, 'which has been administered without a cent of cost to the people, which is supported by old and young alike and which serves a commendable purpose.
In. the report prepared by Doctor Manion reference was made to private organizations collecting money to provide the forces with sporting goods and equipment, but we find that this work is also done by the Y.M.C.A. and other organizations. During the last war we had a very fine organization in Toronto which carried on this work; I refer to the sportsmen's fund. Yet in spite of what is being done by these organizations we find that provision has been made in the estimates of the armed forces for expenditure of up to $175,000 for equipment of this kind. At the end of the fourth year of the war, with very heavy income taxes, business taxes and sales taxes, with nearly $5,000,000 a day being spent on the war, the public are getting sick and tired of all these funds, and their pockets are being drained. When the taxes are paid; when the orders of the controllers and subcontrollers are obeyed, I do not know anyone who has any money left to subscribe in this way.
The minister says these people are very happy about the whole thing. Of course they are happy; they come to Ottawa and sit down on the chesterfields or comfortable chairs we have heard about, put their feet on the rugs we have read about, and ask for a little something extra this year, raising the estimates sky-high. There should be some public control over these charities. I regret to have to say this, but it is in the public interest. I am sorry I have not my file here to-night; I cannot carry it with me all the time, but from what I have seen of this work in some of the camps and some of the services I know there has been duplication. I believe it was the present minister for air who introduced the War Charities Act just before the war session of 1939 concluded, and at that time he said the act would be strictly enforced,

War Appropriation-War Services
that we would not repeat the mistakes we made in the last war, with local funds, provincial funds and federal funds all mixed up, to the detriment of the victory loans. I do not blame these people for being satisfied; of course they should be satisfied. Take the Y.M.C.A.; they are doing very good work, no dou'bt, as all the charities are doing good work, but I contend that there is duplication and waste in connection with some of these funds; duplication of service and waste in connection with overhead charges.
Some of the equipment that has been supplied has been donated without charge. They ' go around the streets and collect equipment of all kinds. No doubt this is done to effect economy, and no doubt they are doing a good work. I am not here to criticize these funds,, because they are supported by public-spirited citizens who go down in their pockets liberally. But I do say that because of the mistakes at the time of the last war there should be more coordination of the funds of these various organizations. No doubt the work they are doing is excellent, but I cannot see why it is necessary to have separate real estate, separate staffs, separate stenographers, separate advertising on the billboards and in the newspapers and all that kind of thing, for seven different funds, with a vote of $7,000,000. If it goes on for another year or two it will be up to $10,000,000. I urge upon the minister that he bring about more coordination in the interests of economy and efficiency, and to protect the taxpayer who, almost every day, has a hat placed in front of him, and is asked to chip in and to subscribe to many different funds for war purposes.

Is the minister responsible for the operation and supervision of canteens? If so, under what item might they be discussed?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	Is the hon. member
referring to canteens operated by military units, or those operated by the auxiliary services? If the former, then that is entirely a regimental matter, and under the control of the Department of National Defence. As I recall-and I hope I am right-they have a special canteen committee which looks after these matters. But that particular kind of canteen does not come under this vote, or under my department.

It is under the Department of National Defence, then?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	If it is a military
canteen, yes.

What about the Navy-Army-Air Force Institute?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	That is a British
organization.

But there is a Canadian Branch?
Mr. LaFLECHE: The N.A.A.F.I. is a British organization, although it may have branches in this country. I am not sure about that. Again I must say it is not in my department.
I wish I had the information, but unfortunately I have not.

Is this $7,000,000 in
addition to moneys which might be raised from drives for funds?
Mr. LaFLECHE: These moneys are given from public funds, in lieu of public subscription. A moment ago the hon. member for Broadview referred to the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire. I might point out that last year of their own accord they preferred to raise funds through public subscription and, of course, their wishes were met. Last year, to the extent of $281,119 the Navy League financed from this vote, for particular wartime purposes. Then they ' went to the public for the funds which they would require in ordinary times, with the possible exception of certain commodities and other things which they require for the men of the sea.

On what basis are these moneys allocated to the various organizations?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	The moneys are paid
following the assignment to a particular piece of work for the armed forces. The association in question puts it into a budget, which is gone over very carefully. When found correct, it is approved by the Minister of National War Services, and in that way the particular task is financed.

At
the present time the Department of National War Services appears to be trying to bring the different auxiliary services in the different cities together under what they call a coordinating war services auxiliary or committee. I understand the department expects that committee to look after the entertainment of soldiers, sailors and airmen in the different cities. Does the department supply the money, or do the cities have to raise that amount?
Mr. LaFLECHE: The hon. member for Peterborough West has referred to local coordinating citizens committees. At the moment they are not financed. Some have requested

War Appropiiation-War Services
consideration of their difficulties in finding relatively small sums of money to pay for postage, for clerks or even for the rental of office space, and that matter is under consideration. At the moment, however, these committees which answer local needs, or which are developed because there is a need for work in a particular community, are supposed at the moment to finance themselves. I might say that, generally speaking, they do not have to spend so much money. I will grant, of course, that if a properly ambitious and patriotic local committee does go in for meeting trains bearing members of the armed forces who pass through a town, or who come to a city or town for a week-end, it would run into considerable money. But in many places there are other organizations to do that work. Coordinating committees are rather well described by the word "coordinating". I trust that is the information the hon. member wants?

In Peterborough we have a recreation centre for the armed forces. This has been carried on by the Kiwanis club, and at least 150,000 men of the armed forces have been entertained in that centre. Other activities in Peterborough are being carried on by other organizations. Do I understand that someone in the Department of National War Services has asked that dances be arranged for the soldiers? Under those circumstances I wonder whether financial arrangements would have to be made locally, or if they would be made by the department. A dance costs a lot of money, if one has to hire an orchestra.
Mr. LaFLECHE: If anyone on behalf of the Department of National War Services has requested that recreational or amusement features be entered into, it is really to answer a need proclaimed by the armed forces themselves. We do many times make known to local communities, through the agency of one organization or another, that at such-and-such a spot the boys are lonesome, and it would be a fine thing if something were done about it. The department does not anticipate organizing dances.

I
placed a question on the order paper in regard to Miss Helen Doherty, and I should like to know if that would come under this item.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Miss Doherty is general assistant in the Department of National War Services.

That matter would be discussed under the civil estimates.
Mr. LaFLECHE: That is right.
[Mr. LaFlecheJ

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Would the women's
volunteer services come under this particular item or under the civil estimates?
Mr. LaFLECHE: That would come under sundry services, not because it is not important but because the treasury board lumped a number of lesser sums together. If the hon. gentleman wishes to discuss the women's volunteer services under this item, I am perfectly happy to have him do so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have no desire to alter the sequence at all.
' Mr. HANSELL: We are being asked to vote $7,000,000 for auxiliary services. Have any of the organizations which would come under this vote made a popular appeal for funds during the past year and, if so, what amounts were collected?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I have stated already that last year the Red Cross went to the country and got over $10,000,000. That was their objective and they got it. Among the organizations that I mentioned is the Navy League which did go to the public for some money. However, that was not to carry on any of the work covered by this item.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Salvage division, $396,965.

At sidings and railway stations of western Canada are to be found hundreds of tons of scrap iron which were collected by voluntary organizations. Some two and a half years ago the government made an appeal for the collection of scrap and passed a regulation which made it illegal to have more than 300 pounds of scrap on any farm. Voluntary organizations collected this scrap metal but, judging from what one sees when travelling on the train, apparently very little of it has been shipped. The result is that many of the organizations have become discouraged after having expended considerable efforts in collecting this scrap.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I believe the hon. member is referring to small quantities of scrap iron. These have been left where they are until some economic arrangement can be worked out to move this scrap material. Throughout Canada there are piles of salvaged materials of one kind and another which have been collected and which are immediately available. The location and availability of these materials are known to those concerned. These piles are a very necessary reserve. Could the hon. gentleman give me more precise details as to the localities, and then I should be glad to have the matter looked

War Appropriation-War Services
into and to give him full information. If it is a matter of two or three hundred pounds-I think the hon. member mentioned that figure -it would hardly be worth shipping.

The three hundred pounds I mentioned had reference to the limit on the amount of scrap which could be left on a farm under the regulations passed by the government. The other scrap I am referring to runs into hundreds of thousands of pounds. These piles of scrap are to be seen at almost every station and on almost every loading platform in western Canada, and the people wonder why it is not being used.
Mr. LaFLECHE: It is these large quantities of scrap which have been gathered together that I had in mind a moment ago. These are reserve piles, and their whereabouts and availability are known. They form part of the inventory of the industry concerned.

A perusal of the figures covering the operations of this particular branch of the Department of National War Services would seem to indicate that the costs are mounting and that we are building up more or less of a bureaucracy. The auditor general's report for the year ended March 31, 1942, shows expenditures in round figures of $160,000. This year it is proposed to spend more than twice this amount, and I should like to have a break-down of this item into the following divisions:
Salaries.
Travelling expenses.
Publicity.
Printing and stationery.
Telegrams and telegraphs.
Miscellaneous.
Mr. LaFLECHE: The break-down I have does not show telegrams separately, but otherwise I think it gives the information desired by the hon. member. Salaries amount to $79,715, which is an increase of $8,715 over last year. The other figures for last year and this year are as follows:
Cost of living bonus.... $ 3,000 Unemployment insurance 250
Travelling expenses		50,000
Printing and stationery. 4,000
Publicity	 250,000
Miscellaneous	 10,000
Last year $ 2,000 130 34,000 3,750 195,000 7,0(50

I think it would be interesting to the committee for me to place on Hansard for purposes of comparison the amount actually expended on this work for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1942. These figures are from the auditor general's report and are the only ones available to me.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I have the figures for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1943, if the hon. gentleman would like them.

Are they authentic, from the auditor general?
Mr. LaFLECHE: They were given to me by the chief treasury officer of my department, and I take them to be correct. May I put them on record?

If the minister would.
Mr. LaFLECHE: These are the expenditures for the fiscal year to March 31, 1943: salaries, $69,636.83; cost of living bonus, $1,813.96; unemployment insurance, $133.45; travelling expenses, $29,580.34; printing and stationery, $9,454.86; publicity, $149,922.18; miscellaneous, $6,419.40; making a total, as given me, of $266,961.02.

I think it would still be of interest for me to place on Hansard for purposes of comparison the expenditures for the previous year, when scrap was more difficult to get.
Mr. LaFLECHE: It is more difficult to get it now.

There is plenty of scrap in the country to-day.
Mr. LaFLECHE: It is more difficult to get it now, and the country needs it so badly.

The expenditures for last year were: salaries, $15,680.22; travelling expenses, $7,342.34; publicity, $127,349.71; printing and stationery, $2,728.97; telegrams and telephones, $854.65; miscellaneous, $5,262.34; making a total of $159,218.23. To-day the figures are more than double that, and I see no justification for such an increase in the amount that is being asked for this year.
Mr. LaFLECHE : I hope I can explain it to the satisfaction of my hon. friend. It has been necessary to go farther afield for many commodities that can be salvaged. The whole of Canada is now pretty well covered, and a greater variety of goods is being collected. It is more difficult now to get the quantities of materials required by the different industries in Canada for the simple reason that the bulk of the salvage has been taken off; the back yards have been cleaned out to a much greater extent than they were two years ago. Junk has been picked up and turned in. Fate and bones, while not a romantic subject, are extremely important in providing glycerine which is necessary in making explosives. We have to ask and train the whole of Canada into a routine to save fate and bones on account of the necessity of making available to the fighting nations explosives which are derived from some of the ingredients of fats and bones. Scrap metals of all kinds are also wanted, and rubber; we are far from being out of the

War Appropriation-War Services
woods in regard to rubber. The time will come, and the quicker the better, when it will not be necessary to ask all the citizens of Canada for the sake of victory to turn in their rubber tires and other articles made of rubber. I agree with the hon. member for Camrose that it is difficult to become enthusiastic about salvage. But these materials are of vital necessity in the war. At one time during this war I had the honour of wearing the king's uniform and it was not so easy, I assure the committee, to change from one role to the other. Yet I must express my deep admiration to the citizens of this country who are doing their best in this way to help win the war. I would not be a party to an extravagant organization, nor would I appear before this house if I did not think salvage was necessary.
One more thing. At this moment in the history of the world money is not worth anything compared with the blood of our boys in Sicily who maybe are being killed to-night.

Hear, hear.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Then let us not hear about money against blood.

I do not want to hold up the item, and it is getting near eleven o'clock. We all agree with what the minister has said about the comparison between blood and money, but I do not really think that enters into the picture at all.
Could the minister give to the committee, perhaps not to-night but some other night, the value of the materials that have been salvaged, because it may be a pretty expensive job if we are spending nearly $400,000 to get these materials? Is a record kept of the value of the salvage at all?
The minister mentioned rubber. The minister perhaps does not travel extensively throughout the country and may not know how much rubber there is lying around this country. I asked the Minister of Munitions and Supply a few weeks ago why this rubber was not being reclaimed, and he said that the reclaiming plants were overstocked now and that we have not enough plants to care for the old rubber we have on hand. I am not overlooking the fact that we may need rubber just the same.
A word about scrap iron. The farmers have hauled in tons and tons of scrap iron to their various communities. They have to do it by the regulations and at their own expense. I am going to suggest to the minister what I suggested to his predecessor, that it would be a magnanimous thing, and yet only what we might expect, if the railway companies

would at least haul that scrap iron free of charge to some central point where it is needed. The few gallons used by the farmer in hauling in the scrap iron means more to him than one carload in a thirty or forty-car train means to the railways. I make that suggestion and I hope the minister will give it consideration. At some future time-I am not asking the minister to do it to-night- I hope he will also tell the committee the value of the salvage that has been collected in this country.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I shall be very happy to put on the record the information desired by the hon. gentleman. I can give a very rough total figure to-night. We have recorded in the books of the department something over 300,000 tons of salvaged material. It is difficult to put a market value on it. I repeat, when you badly need a commodity in war time, if you have the material the cost is of secondary importance. Nevertheless, I shall bring the information down.
